title: Nobel Physics Prize Goes to Francis Halzen for Capturing 'Ghost Particles' From Deep Space
excerpt: The Belgian physicist's decades-long project — thousands of light sensors buried in Antarctic ice — opened a new kind of astronomy based on neutrinos, the elusive 'ghost particles' of the cosmos.
body:
• Belgian physicist Francis Halzen, 82, won the 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics for "decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin," the Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced on Tuesday.
  • Halzen first proposed in 1988 that the clear ice beneath the South Pole could serve as a giant detector; IceCube — thousands of light sensors buried in a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice — was completed at the end of 2010.
  • The prize, worth 12 million Swedish crowns (about $1.2 million), went to a sole winner — a rarity in recent years — and will be presented by Sweden's King Carl XVI Gustaf in Stockholm on December 10.
  • The Nobel committee said Halzen's work opened "a new kind of astronomy," using ghost-like particles that stream through planets, stars and human bodies untouched to map distant galaxies and exploding stars.

The 2026 Nobel Prize in Physics has been awarded to Francis Halzen, the Belgian physicist whose decades-long quest to capture the universe's most elusive particles gave humanity an entirely new way to see the cosmos. The Royal Swedish Academy of Sciences announced the award in Stockholm on Tuesday, honouring Halzen's "decisive contributions to the IceCube Neutrino Observatory and the discovery of high-energy neutrinos of astrophysical origin."

Ghost particles, caught in Antarctic ice

Neutrinos are the ghosts of the particle world: they carry almost no mass and no electric charge, so they can pass through planets, stars and human bodies without being altered. Roughly 100 trillion of them stream through each of us every second. That very elusiveness makes them precious to science — because they travel in straight lines from their sources, untouched by magnetic fields, they carry information about distant galaxies and exploding stars that no other messenger can deliver.

Halzen realised in 1988 that the clear ice beneath the South Pole could act as a detector. On the rare occasion a neutrino strikes an atomic nucleus, it gives off a flash of light — and sensors buried deep in the ice can record it. The first attempt, called AMANDA, was completed in 2000 but proved too small for the task. It was expanded into IceCube, finished at the end of 2010: thousands of light detectors embedded in a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice, with the University of Wisconsin–Madison — where the 82-year-old Halzen is based — as the lead institution.

"Francis Halzen has led an international team of researchers and engineers who have provided us with a fantastic instrument," said Mark Pearce, chair of the Nobel Committee for Physics. "His tenacity and scientific vision has paved the way for a new kind of astronomy."

"People joined him in the quest for these neutrino messengers. The messenger is bringing information from the cosmos. They opened the door to distant galaxies and tell us about the processes of exploding stars."

— Eva Olsson, member of the Nobel Committee for Physics

A surprise four decades in the making

Halzen, who took the committee's call from Italy, said the honour was unexpected even after decades of speculation that he might one day win. "It was a great surprise, and I obviously didn't expect it," he said. "When we started this project, everybody realised this was maybe a good idea but very few thought it would work, including myself. So this was kind of an adventure where success wasn't guaranteed."

Physics Today editor-in-chief Richard Fitzgerald noted that although hundreds of people built the observatory, "it all started with one person" — and the physics prize has rarely gone to a sole winner in recent years. Last year's award went to John Clarke, Michel Devoret and John Martinis for experiments demonstrating quantum physics in action, seen as a step toward next-generation computing.

The physics prize was the second of this year's Nobels to be unveiled, following Monday's medicine prize. The chemistry prize is announced on Wednesday.

Why it matters

Neutrino astronomy has matured from a gamble into a discipline. The high-energy neutrinos IceCube detects are messengers from the most violent events in the universe — processes around black holes, exploding stars and the engines of distant galaxies — and they reveal things light telescopes cannot see. "They give us information which we cannot get in any other way," said Nobel Committee member Eva Lindroth. "It gives a new way to study the universe."

The award also carries a 12 million Swedish crown prize (about $1.2 million). Halzen told the news conference he is working on a new proposal and hopes the prize will help get it approved — drawing chuckles from the audience.

Diaspora angle

The prize is a milestone for international big science, followed closely by research communities worldwide — including India's growing community of physicists and science students. For a generation that has come of age as India expands its own research ambitions, the award spotlights a field — multi-messenger astronomy — where the biggest questions are still wide open.

What's next

Laureates receive their medals from King Carl XVI Gustaf at a ceremony in Stockholm on December 10, the anniversary of Alfred Nobel's death, followed by the traditional banquet at Stockholm City Hall. Meanwhile, physicists will be watching what Halzen's next proposal holds — and whether the "new kind of astronomy" he pioneered can answer the deeper question his detector was built for: where, exactly, in the cosmos these ghost particles are born.
